headline: 英倫兩則六十年回顧
context: 英國衛報這輪刊出兩篇跨越一甲子的回顧文章。一篇作者回憶自己與諾丁丘嘉年華（Notting Hill Carnival）六十年的淵源，從童年的不情願，到音響車進場後成為每年必朝聖的盛會；另一篇是攝影師楊威廉（William Yang）回顧他六十年來記錄LGBTQ+生活的攝影生涯，累積超過五十萬張照片。

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom My earliest memories of the Notting Hill carnival are of being mildly irritated. In its 1960s infancy, the event was strictly a Caribbean affair, transplanted to Ladbroke Grove as authentically as was practical. Its purpose was as obvious as its origins: giving Caribbean arrivals a chance to celebrate themselves by bringing the vibrancy of the home they left behind to these drab streets for a couple of days. Vital as this was – and it really was – it didn’t cut much ice with surly 10- or 11-year-olds like me, being dragged around behind parading steelbands. Yes, it was great to see so many Black people out in the open together and your mums and dads laughing and having a good time, but did we need to be here? There was football to be played and bikes to be ridden, yet so many of us were being forced to walk for what seemed like miles following “old people music”. Continue reading...
sources.title: From ‘old people music’ to owning the streets: 60 years of Notting Hill carnival and me

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past As a young adult, William Yang discovered that his family’s story was actually a murder mystery. His uncle, William Fang Yuen, was killed by an employee on the family’s farm in far north Queensland in 1922, but his mother refused to tell him the full story. In 1990, he travelled to Innisfail in search of the truth. One aunt told Yang that his uncle and the worker had got into a fight over a gambling debt, and the worker had stabbed him to death with a spear. A cousin said a gang was involved. A local woman, who had been a child at the time, remembered it as a card game gone wrong. Continue reading...
sources.title: ‘The whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay’: William Yang on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ life

thread_text: 英國衛報這輪刊出兩篇跨越一甲子的回顧文章。一篇作者回憶自己與諾丁丘嘉年華（Notting Hill Carnival）六十年的淵源——小時候覺得被拖著參加很煩，直到1970年代音響車文化進場，才變成每年必朝聖的自由儀式。另一篇是攝影師楊威廉（William Yang），他從1960年代末移居雪梨後開始拍照，六十年下來累積超過五十萬張照片，如今大半時間都花在整理過去的紀錄。
threads_text: 英國衛報這輪刊出兩篇跨越一甲子的回顧文章，主題都是「一個人跟時間的關係」。第一篇，作者回憶自己與諾丁丘嘉年華六十年的淵源——小時候覺得被大人拖著參加很煩，直到1970年代音響車文化進場，嘉年華才變成她每年一定要去的自由儀式。第二篇，攝影師楊威廉從1960年代末移居雪梨後開始拿起相機，六十年下來累積超過五十萬張照片，如今大半時間都花在整理、追索這些影像背後的故事，包括一樁跟自己家族有關的懸案。
voice_text: 衛報這次端出兩篇跨越一甲子的回憶文章。第一篇，作者聊自己跟諾丁丘嘉年華的六十年淵源——小時候覺得被拖著參加很煩，直到七零年代音響車文化進場，才變成每年一定要去的自由儀式。第二篇，攝影師楊威廉，從六零年代末搬到雪梨開始拍照，六十年下來拍了超過五十萬張照片，現在大半時間都在整理過去。
